title: The saint-soldier
hook: the Khalsa ideal holds prayer and courage together in one person
tomorrow: Two flags at the Akal Takht

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Rehat Maryada, and your line, a shared code. That closed our days on the Sikh way of life. Today a new stretch begins: sword and saint. Day two hundred seventy-four.

At dawn, someone sits cross-legged, eyes closed, lips moving with a prayer. Later that day, someone stands between a bully and the kid being bullied, and doesn't step aside. It's easy to file them in different drawers. The quiet one and the brave one. The monk and the firefighter. The Sikh tradition keeps asking a stubborn question: why not the same person? Why not someone who prays at dawn and, when it's needed, stands in the doorway? Today: the saint-soldier.
screen: `ONE PRAYS AT DAWN.` → `ONE STANDS IN THE DOORWAY.` → `WHY NOT THE SAME PERSON?`

segments.voice: Sant is a saint, a holy person, someone whose mind rests in God. Sipahi is a soldier. It's a Persian word, and the English word sepoy comes from it. Put them together, sant sipahi, and you have a phrase Sikhs often use for the Khalsa ideal. The idea has a history. The first Gurus were teachers of the Name, poets and farmers. Then, in 1606, the fifth Guru, Guru Arjan, was executed in Lahore by the Mughal authorities. His son, Guru Hargobind, became the sixth Guru as a boy, and tradition says he put on two swords. One he called miri, worldly responsibility. The other he called piri, spiritual authority. Both, worn at once. Nearly a century later, Guru Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa in 1699 and gave the idea its fullest form. The Khalsa would keep the daily prayers and the discipline of the Name, and also stand ready to protect the weak and resist injustice. Notice the order. The saint comes first in the phrase, and in the life. The daily prayers aren't a warm-up before the real work. They're the root, and courage grows out of them. Without the saint, the soldier is only force. Without the soldier, the saint may watch injustice and do nothing. Sikhs don't read this as a call to go looking for fights. A saint-soldier may never touch a weapon beyond the small kirpan. Their courage looks like telling the truth in a meeting, or refusing to laugh along. The prayer steadies them. The courage makes it real.
screen: `SANT — SAINT. SIPAHI — SOLDIER.` · `1606: TWO SWORDS, MIRI AND PIRI.` · `1699: THE KHALSA HOLDS BOTH.` · `THE SAINT COMES FIRST.` · then, large: `SAINT AND SOLDIER.`

segments.voice: Two halves, then. First, the saint. Sit still and settle. If you pray, you can use a line you know. If not, just rest your mind on something good and true for a few breaths. Then, the soldier. Bring to mind one small brave thing waiting for you today: a hard conversation, a truth to tell, someone to stand beside. Don't do it yet. Just decide you will, from this steady place. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Sant sipahi. The saint-soldier: prayer and courage held together in one person, with the saint first.
Your line: saint and soldier. Today, pray or pause first, then do the one brave thing you decided on. Day two hundred seventy-four.

original.note: Gurmukhi: sant, saint; sipahi, soldier, a word from Persian.

trapdoor: what you thought: a warrior who also prays sometimes.
what it means: one person in whom prayer and courage grow together, with the prayer as the root.
what a scholar hears: sipahi is Persian (the source of sepoy); the pairing goes back to Guru Hargobind's miri and piri after Guru Arjan's execution in 1606, and to the Khalsa of 1699.

notes: The phrase 'sant sipahi' is a widely used later formulation of the Khalsa ideal rather than a term found in the Guru Granth Sahib; confirm framing.
Guru Arjan's execution in Lahore, 1606, under Mughal authority (Jahangir); Guru Hargobind's age at succession (about 11) left unstated.
Sepoy derived from Persian sipahi: standard etymology; confirm.
